issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may reverse an acquittal only after giving due weight to the reinforced presumption of innocence and finding sufficient reason to displace a plausible view of the evidence.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after finding it unsafe to rely on the principal witnesses and considering the evidence as a whole.
The High Court reappraised the evidence and reversed the acquittal, but the Supreme Court found the trial court’s view plausible and no compelling circumstances requiring reversal.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have reversed the acquittal; the acquittal was restored.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court has plenary power and a duty to review the evidence in an appeal against acquittal, and the Code of Criminal Procedure does not curtail that power. However, the accused has a double presumption of innocence after acquittal; if two reasonable conclusions are possible, the appellate court should not disturb the acquittal. Reversal requires substantial and compelling circumstances and an absolute assurance of guilt, not merely a different possible view. The Court relied on Shivaji Sahebrao Bobade v. State of Maharashtra, Girija Prasad v. State of M.P., State of Goa v. Sanjay Thakran, Chandrappa v. State of Karnataka, and State of Rajasthan v. Shera Ram.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and trial_court_view_plausible and not compelling_reversal_reasons

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a trial court’s acquittal.
predicates.trial_court_view_plausible: The trial court assessed the evidence and reached a view that is reasonably available on that evidence.
predicates.compelling_reversal_reasons: The evidence or circumstances provide substantial and compelling grounds to displace the acquittal.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal, a plausible trial court view without compelling grounds for reversal means the acquittal should not be reversed.

issues.legal_issue: A competent and reliable child witness may provide the basis for a criminal conviction without mandatory corroboration, although corroboration is a matter of prudence.
material_facts: The principal alleged eyewitness was eleven years old at the time of the incident.
The High Court relied on her testimony, while the trial court considered it unsafe to do so in light of the circumstances and the conduct of the witnesses.
issues.conclusion: A child witness’s evidence can by itself support a conviction if it is credible and reliable; corroboration is desirable as a matter of prudence but is not an inflexible legal requirement.
issues.legal_principle: A child witness must be competent and reliable, and the court must consider whether the witness may have been tutored. There is no rule requiring corroboration in every case, though a court may prudently seek support from other dependable evidence. The Court relied on Dattu Ramrao Sakhare v. State of Maharashtra, Panchhi v. State of U.P., Prakash v. State of M.P., Baby Kandayanathil v. State of Kerala, Raja Ram Yadav v. State of Bihar, and State of U.P. v. Ashok Dixit.

rule.if: criminal_conviction_case and child_witness_competent and child_testimony_reliable and not likelihood_of_tutoring

predicates.criminal_conviction_case: The proceeding concerns whether evidence can sustain a criminal conviction.
predicates.child_witness_competent: A child witness is capable of understanding questions and giving evidence about the events witnessed.
predicates.child_testimony_reliable: The child’s testimony is credible and truthful in the circumstances of the case.
predicates.likelihood_of_tutoring: There is a likelihood that the child witness was tutored.

issues.definition: In a criminal conviction case, competent and reliable testimony from a child with no likelihood of tutoring can support a conviction without mandatory corroboration.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s reaction must be assessed in the circumstances, and conduct that is absolutely unnatural may make the witness’s testimony unworthy of credit.
material_facts: The child said she told her maternal grandmother that her mother had been forcibly taken away and threatened.
The grandmother searched for the missing woman but did not tell other family members, anyone in the village, or the police, and remained silent for almost two days.
The Supreme Court considered the trial court justified in viewing this conduct as unnatural and in treating reliance on the witnesses’ testimony as unsafe.
issues.conclusion: The trial court was justified in treating the witnesses’ conduct as unnatural in the circumstances and finding their testimony unsafe to rely on.
issues.legal_principle: Witnesses do not react uniformly, and their behaviour must be assessed in the context of the facts; there is no fixed rule of natural reaction. Nevertheless, conduct that is absolutely unnatural in the circumstances may undermine the credibility of testimony. The Court relied on Gopal Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh, Rana Partap v. State of Haryana, State of H.P. v. Mast Ram, and Lahu Kamlakar Patil v. State of Maharashtra.

predicates.criminal_witness_credibility_assessment: The proceeding requires the court to assess the credibility of a witness in a criminal case.
predicates.conduct_assessed_in_context: The court assesses the witness’s conduct in light of the circumstances and the individual situation.
predicates.conduct_absolutely_unnatural: The witness’s conduct is so inconsistent with the circumstances that it is absolutely unnatural.

issues.definition: In assessing credibility in a criminal case, conduct found absolutely unnatural after contextual assessment may mean the witness’s testimony is rejected as unworthy of credence.
